Block Party

Help residents see—and shape—their neighborhood’s future

A simulation-based civic prototype for Bloomington residents.

  • Civic design
  • Participatory design
  • Interaction design

Block Party is my HCI/d capstone thesis at Indiana University Bloomington. It explores how younger residents could understand urban proposals and contribute ideas through a simulated neighborhood.

The design challenge extends to planners: participation needs to produce input they can interpret and trust.

6 residents tested the prototype

They saw it as valuable, inclusive, and potentially useful for community engagement. This is qualitative prototype feedback; participation growth was not measured.

On this page
The problemResearchDesign journeyParticipationTestingPrototypeReflection

Participation starts with understanding a place.

Block Party focuses on the connection between seeing a possible neighborhood change and expressing an informed opinion about it. A proposal needs enough context for residents to understand what could change and how to respond.

More submissions alone would not demonstrate a better planning process. The experience also needs to consider how planners make sense of resident input.

Resident and planning perspectives, together.

The capstone combined secondary research and digital ethnography across Reddit, public forums, and government websites with interviews, a participatory workshop, and prototype testing.

Monisha participated separately.

A paper-prototype comparison also involved 2 city planners and 2 users. These are activity-specific counts; participants may overlap and are not presented as a combined total.

Put the proposal in its neighborhood.

The virtual map and street-view option connect planning proposals to a spatial setting. Residents can explore the neighborhood, locate a project, and inspect its details before deciding how to participate.

Offer more than one way to contribute.

Residents can vote, comment, and upload an image in response to a proposal. A separate builder lets them assemble an idea from prefabricated elements, then save a draft or submit it.

Make choices—and their results—easier to notice.

Testing identified two practical refinements.

Builder discoverability

Organize prefab elements.

Clearer categories could help residents choose an element based on its function and relevance to a project.

Feedback after an action

Emphasize a proposal’s arrival.

When the page changes, draw attention to the proposed design appearing in an empty plot so residents can recognize the result.

These are testing findings and proposed improvements. A completed revision or retest is not documented.

Inclusion needs more than an inviting interface.

The next iteration needs to address residents’ comfort with digital interfaces, planners’ ability to interpret conflicting submissions, and officials’ confidence that feedback is valid and representative.

I would test these questions with residents and planning stakeholders alongside the interface refinements.
